title: Mechanics and materials: forces, motion and machines
hook: A motor drives a pump through a gearbox that slows the shaft down. Why is the slow shaft coming out usually thicker than the fast motor shaft going in?
oneBreath: Mechanics is about what forces do. Held still, forces balance, in their pushes and in their turning effects, and they load the parts that carry them, which stretch a little and, loaded too far, bend for good or break; unbalanced, they change how things move, and a force moved through a distance does work, at a rate called power. Turned into rotation, the same ideas explain why a motor takes time to run up, how shafts and gears carry its power to a pump, and why a machine out of balance shakes.

ideas.title: Forces in balance
ideas.oneLine: Drawing every force on one object and making them balance shows why each leg of a two-leg sling pulls harder as the legs spread.

ideas.title: Moments and beams
ideas.oneLine: Taking moments, force times its distance at right angles, about one support of a loaded beam finds what each support carries.

ideas.title: Stress, strain and how materials fail
ideas.oneLine: A tensile test's stress-strain curve, force per area against stretch per length, shows a material's stiffness, its yield and its strength as different things.

ideas.title: Motion and Newton's laws
ideas.oneLine: A net force changes how something moves rather than keeping it moving: net force equals mass times acceleration.

ideas.title: Work, energy and power
ideas.oneLine: Work is force times distance and power is the rate of doing it, so a slower lift does the same work at less power.

ideas.title: Rotation: torque, inertia and run-up
ideas.oneLine: A steady net torque raises a shaft's speed steadily, at a rate set by its moment of inertia: its mass and how far out it sits.

ideas.title: Shafts, couplings, belts and gears
ideas.oneLine: Gears and belts trade speed for torque by their ratio, while the power through them stays the same less a small loss.

ideas.title: Vibration, resonance and balance
ideas.oneLine: An unbalanced rotor shakes its mounts hardest at its critical speed, where its turning rate matches the rate the mounts swing at on their own.

calibration.q: A heavy crate sits on a deck. You push it sideways gently and it does not move. How big is the friction holding it?
options: Exactly as big as your push
Its full maximum, however gently you push
calibration.why: It matches your push. Nothing moves, so the forces on the crate balance: friction grows to match the push, up to a limit, and only past that does the crate slip. With no push there is no friction at all, so it is not always at its maximum.

calibration.q: A light 4 m beam rests on two trestles, one at each end. A loaded chain block hangs 1 m from the left end. Which trestle carries more?
options: The left trestle, nearer the block
Both the same, half the load each
The right trestle, which has more beam on its side
calibration.why: The left, three-quarters of the load. Take moments about the left trestle: the load sits 1 m out, so the right trestle, 4 m away, needs only a quarter of it to balance. The long side gives the far trestle more leverage, so it needs less force.
